prompts.speaking.goal.short: Help me define the goal of my talk on “[topic]”.
prompts.speaking.goal.detailed: I'm preparing a [minutes]-minute talk on “[topic]” for [audience]. Help me state the goal in one sentence: “after the talk, listeners will know / be able to / decide…”. Suggest 3 options: inform, persuade, teach. For each, what it changes about the content.
prompts.speaking.goal.refine: The goal is too big for [minutes] minutes. Narrow it down.
prompts.speaking.goal.check: Here's my talk outline: [outline]. Does every point serve the goal “[goal]”? What's unnecessary?
prompts.speaking.audience.short: What should I consider when presenting “[topic]” to [audience]?
prompts.speaking.audience.detailed: Help me describe the audience for a talk on “[topic]”: [who the listeners are]. Answer: what they probably already know, what they find confusing, what matters to them, what questions or doubts they may have, which words and examples to avoid. End with 3 tips for adapting the talk.
prompts.speaking.audience.refine: The room will have both beginners and experts. How do I keep it interesting for both?
prompts.speaking.audience.check: Here's my opening paragraph: [text]. Does it suit [audience]?
prompts.speaking.structure.short: Suggest a structure for a [minutes]-minute talk on “[topic]”.
prompts.speaking.structure.detailed: Make a talk structure: topic “[topic]”, goal “[goal]”, time [minutes] minutes. Blocks: opening, 2–4 main parts, closing. For each: what to say, which example or data to use, how many minutes. Add transition phrases between parts.
prompts.speaking.structure.refine: I've been given 3 minutes less. What can I cut without losing the point?
prompts.speaking.structure.check: Here's my structure: [structure]. Is it clear where I'm taking the audience?
prompts.speaking.opening.short: Suggest 3 ways to open and close a talk on “[topic]”.
prompts.speaking.opening.detailed: For a talk on “[topic]” to [audience], suggest 3 openings: a question to the room, a short story, a problem from the listeners' lives. And 3 closings: a one-line takeaway, a call to action, a return to the opening. No made-up facts or quotes. Each option no longer than 3 sentences.
prompts.speaking.opening.refine: Make option [number] simpler and more natural, as if I'm talking to friends.
prompts.speaking.opening.check: My opening and closing: [text]. Do they connect to each other and to the goal?
prompts.speaking.slides.detailed: Lay the material out as slides for a [minutes]-minute talk. For each slide: a headline that makes a claim (not just a topic), 1–3 short points or an idea for an image, what I say out loud. No more than 25 words on a slide. Material: [material]
prompts.speaking.slides.refine: Where would a chart work better than text? What type of chart should I use?
prompts.speaking.slides.check: Here are my slide headlines: [headlines]. Reading only these, is the story clear?
prompts.speaking.overloaded.short: Cut this slide down to 3 points: [slide text]
prompts.speaking.overloaded.detailed: This slide is overloaded: [slide text]. Produce: a headline stating the conclusion in one phrase, no more than 3 points of 5–7 words, and separately — what to move into the spoken part, what could be shown as an image or diagram, what to cut entirely.
prompts.speaking.overloaded.refine: Split this slide into two if that's clearer.
prompts.speaking.overloaded.check: New version of the slide: [text]. Can it be understood in 5 seconds?
prompts.speaking.notes.short: Write speaker notes for these slides: [slides]
prompts.speaking.notes.detailed: Write speaker notes for each slide: 3–5 keywords, the main point in one phrase, the transition to the next slide, rough timing. No continuous text: I want to speak in my own words, not read. Slides: [slides]
prompts.speaking.notes.refine: Add marks for where to pause and where to ask the room a question.
prompts.speaking.notes.check: I'll talk through slide [number]; tell me if I missed the main point: [what I said]
prompts.speaking.example.short: Come up with a clear example for this idea: [idea]
prompts.speaking.example.detailed: I need to explain a complex idea to [audience]: [idea]. Suggest 4 options: a comparison with an everyday situation, a mini story, a visual demonstration, a numerical example. For each, note where it simplifies the idea and how it might mislead.
prompts.speaking.example.refine: Example [number] is good but long. Cut it to 2 sentences.
prompts.speaking.example.check: Here's my example: [example]. What might a listener misunderstand?
prompts.speaking.rehearsal.short: Make a rehearsal plan for my talk over [days] days.
prompts.speaking.rehearsal.detailed: The talk is in [days] days and lasts [minutes] minutes. Make a rehearsal plan: by day, what to practise (structure, opening and closing, transitions, timing, answering questions), how to check myself (timer, recording, a listener). Bear in mind it's best not to rehearse much on the day itself.
prompts.speaking.rehearsal.refine: I get very nervous. Add exercises to the plan that help me speak more calmly.
prompts.speaking.rehearsal.check: In rehearsal I took [time] instead of [minutes] minutes. What should I speed up or cut?
prompts.speaking.qa.short: What questions might I get after a talk on “[topic]”?
prompts.speaking.qa.detailed: Here's a summary of my talk: [summary]. Audience: [audience]. Write 8 likely questions: clarifying, critical, “what if”, personal. For each, suggest how to answer in 30 seconds and what to do if I don't know the answer.
prompts.speaking.qa.refine: Ask me the questions one at a time as a sceptical listener.
prompts.speaking.qa.check: My answer to question [number]: [answer]. Is it short and to the point?

verify.speaking.goal: The goal should be yours. If the AI's wording sounds good but isn't what you want, rewrite it.
verify.speaking.audience: The AI doesn't know your audience. If you can, ask the organiser or a couple of listeners what they already know.
verify.speaking.structure: Run through the structure out loud with a timer: on paper it often seems shorter than it is.
verify.speaking.opening: Don't open with made-up statistics or a “surprising fact” without a source. Check every number.
verify.speaking.slides: A slide supports your speech, it doesn't replace it. If a slide makes sense without you, it has too much text.
verify.speaking.overloaded: Check that no important caveats or numbers were lost in the cut.
verify.speaking.notes: Notes are cues, not a script. If you're reading them off the page, cut them to keywords.
verify.speaking.example: An example must be accurate, not just easy to follow. Check the comparison doesn't distort the idea.
verify.speaking.rehearsal: The best check is recording yourself on your phone and watching it. The AI can't hear your voice or pace.
verify.speaking.qa: If you don't know the answer to a question, say so honestly and offer to follow up later. Don't make things up.
